source: 1968 Chevrolet Chassis Service Manual, Brakes, p.5-28

procedures.title: Disc brake caliper: remove, overhaul and install
steps: Take care not to catch the boots on the disc edge while lowering the caliper on (see figure 42 in the manual).
Bolt the caliper to the mounting bracket with the 2 hex head bolts (torque per the specifications at the back of the manual).
Install the shoes and linings as described under Brake Shoes.
Corvette front caliper: put a new copper gasket on the male end of the hose. Screw the hose into the caliper and, with wheels straight ahead, feed its female end through the support bracket.
Check the tube seat is clean, connect the brake line tube nut to the caliper and tighten securely.

Let the hose take its natural, untwisted position, seat the fitting hex in the bracket's 12-point hole and lock it with the U-shaped retainer. Steer lock to lock and watch that the hose touches nothing through suspension and steering travel; if it does, remove the retainer, turn the hose end one or two points to clear, refit and recheck. When good, thread the steel tube connector into the hose fitting and tighten securely.
Rear caliper: connect the brake line to the caliper.
Refit the wheels and lower the car.
notes: CAUTION: reused shoes must go back in their original positions. New shoes carry an arrow on the back showing forward disc rotation.
CAUTION: do not move the car until the pedal is firm.

procedures.title: Brake disc: check runout, remove and install
steps: (Front runout check) Tighten the wheel bearing adjusting nut until all play is gone but the wheel still just turns. Clamp a dial indicator to the caliper with its button on the disc about 1 in. from the outer edge (see figure 43 in the manual).
notes: Disc service is very critical because of the machining tolerances. Excess runout knocks the pistons back, giving more pedal travel and vibration when braking.
Machining the discs is not recommended. Once a wear pattern is established, discs are less prone to scoring problems than drums.
Replace a disc that is thinner than the minimum; a thinner disc can let the shoes come out of contact with the shoe abutments and malfunction.
